vignette:
She is a 52-year-old South Eastern Asian woman who has been married for many years and works in fast food, a job that keeps her on her feet for long shifts and demands a steady pace even when she feels worn down. Before the disaster, her life is busy but familiar. She rises early, prepares what she can for her family, and goes to work with the quiet discipline that has carried her through most of adulthood. She is proud of being reliable. People at work know her as someone who does not complain much, who keeps moving, who can handle a rush at the counter without letting on when she is tired.

That steadiness changes during a natural disaster that comes suddenly and overwhelms the neighborhood where she lives. In the middle of ordinary tasks, the world turns violent. She remembers the noise first: not just wind or rain, but the force of it, the way the sounds seem to come from every direction at once. The house shakes. Objects crash. She thinks in fragments, mostly about her family and the possibility that she will not be able to protect them. There is a sense that time splits open; what happens next feels both immediate and unreal. She does what needs to be done, but later she cannot arrange the sequence of events clearly in her mind. What stays with her is fear so intense that it seems to hollow her out.

Afterward, when the danger has passed, she expects to feel relief. Instead, she finds herself living in a state of alertness that does not switch off. She checks the weather often, then checks again. If the sky darkens, her body reacts before her thoughts do. Her chest tightens, her hands grow damp, and she feels a rush of dread that seems out of proportion to what is happening in the moment. She begins to sit where she can see exits. She notices the sounds of heavy rain or strong wind in a way she never did before, as if her body has learned to brace for impact before her mind can reassure her.

Sleep becomes difficult. She falls asleep exhausted, then wakes abruptly from dreams that replay the disaster in pieces. Sometimes the dreams are not exact memories but variations of them, each one carrying the same terror. When she wakes, she has to orient herself again to the room, to her husband beside her, to the fact that the house is still standing. Even then, her body stays tense, as though it cannot trust the quiet. Some nights she stays awake listening, and the listening itself becomes a kind of suffering.

At work, she tries to maintain the same dependable rhythm, but the environment presses on her nerves in small, relentless ways. The sound of an exhaust fan, the sudden clang of a metal tray, even a customer speaking sharply can make her jump. She becomes more irritable than she wants to be. She feels embarrassed by this and tries to hide it, but the effort takes energy. During busy hours, she sometimes loses her place in tasks she knows well, as though her mind slips away for a moment to scan for danger. She hates that this happens. She has always valued being competent, and now she worries that others notice how strained she seems.

She also finds herself avoiding reminders of the disaster, though she does not think of it in those terms. She does not like storms on television. She changes the channel when coverage shows damaged homes or flooded streets. If the weather report predicts severe conditions, she feels a heavy, sinking fear that can last all day. Her husband encourages her to talk about what happened, but she has trouble finding words that feel complete. Part of her believes that speaking about it might make the memory stronger, more real. Another part feels ashamed that, even now, she can be reduced so quickly to fear.

Over time, she becomes more isolated in the way she carries things. She still goes to work, still cares for her household, still fulfills what is expected, but much of it is done with effort that others do not see. She moves through the day with a sense that she is no longer fully settled in her own life. The disaster is over, yet it remains active in her body and mind, returning in sounds, images, and sudden waves of alarm that make ordinary moments feel unstable.
